stem: What is an **allele**?

options.content: One of the alternative forms of a gene
options.rationale: Correct: e.g. the polled and horned forms of one gene.

options.content: A thread of DNA carrying many genes in a line
options.rationale: That describes a chromosome.

options.content: The observable features of an organism
options.rationale: That is the phenotype.

options.content: A cell with one set of chromosomes
options.rationale: That describes a haploid cell, such as a gamete.

explanation: Alleles are different versions of the same gene at the same position on a chromosome pair.

stem: Which genotype is **heterozygous**?

options.rationale: Two identical dominant alleles: homozygous dominant.
Two identical recessive alleles: homozygous recessive.

options.content: T: a single allele for tall
options.rationale: A single allele is found in a gamete, not a body cell.

options.content: Tt: one tall and one dwarf allele
options.rationale: Correct: two different alleles.

explanation: Heterozygous means two different alleles of a gene.

stem: Two heterozygous tall plants (Tt × Tt) are crossed. What ratio of tall to dwarf offspring is expected?

options.rationale: 1:1 comes from Tt × tt.
Correct: TT, Tt, Tt are tall; tt is dwarf.
All tall comes from TT × any genotype.
This reverses the ratio.

explanation: Tt × Tt gives 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt, so 3 tall : 1 dwarf.

stem: A polled bull is mated with horned cows (polled is dominant). Half the calves are horned. What is the bull's genotype?

options.rationale: A PP bull would give only polled calves.
A pp bull would be horned.
Correct: he passes p to half the calves, giving pp.
A body cell has two alleles, not one.

explanation: Pp × pp gives 1 Pp (polled) : 1 pp (horned).

stem: Which gametes can be produced by an animal with the genotype Bb?

options.rationale: Correct: each gamete carries one allele.
A gamete carries one allele, not two.
Half the gametes carry b.
Gametes are haploid, with one allele each.

explanation: Meiosis separates the two alleles, so half the gametes carry B and half carry b.

stem: In rabbits, black coat (B) is dominant to brown (b). A breeder wants to know whether a black buck is BB or Bb. Which mating is the best test cross?

options.content: Mate him with pure black does
options.rationale: All young would be black whatever his genotype.
Correct: brown does reveal any b allele from the buck.

options.content: Mate him with black carrier does
options.rationale: Possible, but harder to interpret than a cross with bb does.

options.content: Mate him with his own black daughters
options.rationale: This is inbreeding and is not the standard test cross.

explanation: A test cross uses a homozygous recessive partner, so each offspring shows the allele from the unknown parent.
hints: Which does can only give a recessive allele?

stem: Among the polled offspring of a Pp × Pp cross, what fraction is expected to be heterozygous?

options.rationale: Half of all offspring are Pp, but the question asks about polled ones only.
One-quarter of all offspring are PP or pp.
Three-quarters of all offspring are polled.
Correct: of PP, Pp, Pp, two of the three polled are Pp.

explanation: Polled offspring are 1 PP : 2 Pp, so 2/3 are heterozygous carriers of horned.
hints: List the polled genotypes from the Punnett square: PP, Pp, Pp.

stem: Two black cattle produce a red calf (black is dominant to red). What can be concluded?

options.content: One parent must be homozygous BB
options.rationale: A BB parent could not give a b allele.

options.content: The red calf must be a mutation
options.rationale: Two carriers explain it simply.
Correct: a bb calf needs one b from each parent.

options.content: The environment turned the calf red
options.rationale: Coat colour here is controlled by the alleles.

explanation: The red calf is bb, so it received b from each black parent; both are Bb.
hints: What genotype must the red calf have?

stem: A recessive allele shows its effect only when the organism is homozygous for it.
explanation: True. With one dominant allele present, the dominant phenotype appears.

stem: Animals with the same phenotype always have the same genotype.
explanation: False. PP and Pp animals both look polled; a test cross is needed to tell them apart.

stem: Match each term with its meaning.

right.content: Two identical alleles of a gene
Shows its effect even when only one copy is present
A length of DNA controlling one characteristic

explanation: These are the terms both syllabuses require you to define.

stem: Complete the sentences about the cross Bb × bb.

payload.template: The bb parent can only produce gametes carrying the allele {{blank:a}}. The offspring are expected in the ratio {{blank:b}} black to red. This kind of cross with a homozygous recessive is called a {{blank:c}} cross.

explanation: bb gives only b gametes; Bb × bb gives 1:1; a cross with a homozygous recessive is a test cross.

stem: State the term for an organism that has two identical alleles of a gene.
explanation: Two identical alleles: **homozygous** (true-breeding).

stem: Heterozygous tall bean plants (Tt) are self-pollinated and 160 offspring grow. How many are expected to be dwarf?
explanation: Tt × Tt gives 3 tall : 1 dwarf, so dwarf = 1/4 × 160 = 40.
workedSolution: 1. Tt × Tt gives 3 tall : 1 dwarf, so dwarf = 1/4 × 160 = 40.

stem: A heterozygous black buck (Bb) is mated with red does (bb) and 48 kids are born. How many red kids are expected?
explanation: Bb × bb gives 1 black : 1 red, so red = 1/2 × 48 = 24.
workedSolution: 1. Bb × bb gives 1 black : 1 red, so red = 1/2 × 48 = 24.

stem: What percentage of the offspring of a Tt × Tt cross is expected to be homozygous recessive?
explanation: 1 out of 4 offspring is tt: 1 ÷ 4 × 100 = 25%.
hints: Draw the Punnett square and count tt.

stem: In cattle, polled (P) is dominant to horned (p). Using a genetic diagram, show the expected offspring of a cross between a heterozygous polled bull and a horned cow.

points.description: Parental genotypes: Pp × pp.
Gametes: P and p from the bull; p from the cow.
Offspring genotypes: Pp and pp (in equal numbers).
Phenotypes: polled and horned in a 1:1 ratio.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Parents: polled bull Pp × horned cow pp. Gametes: P, p and p. Offspring: Pp, Pp, pp, pp, i.e. 1 polled : 1 horned.

explanation: One mark for each stage of the diagram.
hints: Parents, gametes, Punnett square, genotypes, phenotypes, ratio.

stem: Explain why knowing the genotype of breeding animals is important to a stud breeder.

points.description: Animals with the dominant phenotype may carry a hidden recessive allele (heterozygous).
Carriers can pass unwanted characteristics (e.g. horns or defects) to offspring.
Knowing genotypes (e.g. by test crosses) lets the breeder keep and sell true-breeding (homozygous) stock and cull carriers.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A polled bull may be Pp and carry the horned allele, which he passes to half his calves. Test crosses reveal such carriers, so the breeder can keep only homozygous animals and sell stock that breeds true.

explanation: Hidden alleles, risk, solution.
hints: Think about hidden recessive alleles and selling pure-breeding stock.

stem:
In cattle, black coat (B) is dominant to red coat (b). A breeder kept these records.

| Mating | Black calves | Red calves |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Black bull 'Dumbu' × red cows | 18 | 0 |
| Black bull 'Shumba' × red cows | 9 | 11 |
| F1 black × F1 black (from many matings) | 63 | 21 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: State the genotype of the red cows.
parts.explanation: Red is recessive, so red cows are bb.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: State the most likely genotype of the bull Dumbu.
parts.explanation: No red calves in 18: most likely BB.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: State the genotype of the bull Shumba.
parts.explanation: Red calves appeared, so he carries b: Bb.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate the ratio of black to red calves in the F1 × F1 matings, as black ÷ red.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Draw a genetic diagram to explain the result of the F1 × F1 matings.

points.description: Parents: Bb × Bb.
Gametes: B and b from each parent.
Offspring genotypes: 1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb.
Phenotypes: 3 black : 1 red.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Explain why the breeder cannot be completely certain that Dumbu is BB.

points.description: A Bb bull would give a red calf with each red cow only half of the time (by chance).
So even 18 black calves is a strong indication but not proof; more matings make it more certain.

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: Suggest why the breeder carried out these matings with red cows.

points.description: It is a test cross: red cows (bb) can only give b.
So any red calf reveals that the bull carries b, letting the breeder choose a pure-breeding (BB) bull.

explanation: Use phenotypes of offspring to deduce genotypes; F1 × F1 gives 3:1 and a test cross reveals carriers.
hints: A test cross uses homozygous recessive partners.

stem: In a plant, tall (T) is dominant to dwarf (t). A farmer crosses two tall plants and gets some dwarf offspring.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: State the genotype of the dwarf offspring.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: State the genotype of both tall parents.
parts.explanation: Each gave a t allele, so both are Tt.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain how two tall parents can produce dwarf offspring.

points.description: Each parent carries a hidden recessive allele t (heterozygous).
A dwarf offspring receives t from both parents (tt).

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Suggest how the farmer could obtain a true-breeding tall line.

points.description: Self-pollinate tall plants and keep seed only from those whose offspring are all tall.
Repeat over several generations (or test-cross with tt plants) to keep only TT plants.

explanation: Dwarf offspring from tall parents reveal heterozygous carriers.
hints: What genotype is a dwarf plant?

stem: A farmer selects his breeding cattle only by their appearance. Discuss the strengths and weaknesses of this method using your knowledge of genotype and phenotype.

points.description: Strength: appearance (phenotype) shows dominant characteristics and conformation, quickly and cheaply.
Strength: removing animals with an unwanted recessive phenotype (e.g. horned) reduces that allele over time.
Weakness: heterozygous carriers look like homozygous dominant animals, so recessive alleles stay hidden in the herd.
Weakness: appearance is affected by the environment (feeding, disease), so a good-looking animal may have poor genes and vice versa.
Improvement: use test crosses, performance and progeny records alongside appearance.
Judgement: appearance is a useful first screen but not enough on its own.

levels.descriptor: Accurate, well-developed explanation of several relevant points using correct agricultural terms, applied to the crop, animal or situation in the question, with a clear judgement where one is asked for.
Some relevant points explained, partly developed or only partly applied to the situation; any judgement is simple or one-sided.
Simple statements or a list of points with little explanation or application.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Selecting by appearance is quick and cheap, and it does remove animals that show unwanted recessive features, such as horns, so that allele slowly becomes rarer. However, phenotype does not show genotype: a Pp bull looks exactly like a PP bull, so carriers of horns stay hidden and pass the allele on. Appearance is also affected by the environment: a well-fed animal with average genes may look better than a poorly fed animal with excellent genes. The farmer should add test crosses and records of growth, fertility and offspring. Appearance is a useful first step but not a reliable method on its own.

explanation: Weigh phenotype selection against hidden genotypes and environment.
hints: What can and cannot be seen?
How does the environment affect appearance?
